## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0545-virtual-environments-python-uv-exact-pins.qmd >}}

## What `uv add` writes by default

In [uv: projects](0530-virtual-environments-python-uv-projects.qmd),
`uv add` wrote a *lower bound* for each package.
Here is a fresh project after `uv add pandas`:

```bash
uv add pandas
```

```out
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 5 packages in 19ms
Installed 4 packages in 65ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
```

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
name = "pins-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]
```

`pandas>=3.1.1` declares "pandas 3.1.1 or anything newer".
The exact version you got is still written down,
but only in `uv.lock`:

```{.toml filename="uv.lock"}
[[package]]
name = "pandas"
version = "3.1.1"
```

So the project *declares* a range and *locks* one version.
As long as everyone runs `uv sync` against that `uv.lock`,
everyone gets pandas 3.1.1.

## Why an analysis project declares exact versions

The range in `pyproject.toml` matters whenever the lockfile is not the thing being read.

- **The lockfile gets regenerated.**
  `uv lock --upgrade`, a deleted `uv.lock`,
  or a merge conflict resolved by re-locking
  lets every package move anywhere inside its range,
  and nothing in `pyproject.toml` records that the analysis was run with 3.1.1.
- **People read `pyproject.toml`, not `uv.lock`.**
  It is short enough to read in a code review or a README.
  `pandas==3.1.1` says what the analysis was run with,
  and `pandas>=3.1.1` does not.
- **Other tools read `pyproject.toml` too.**
  `pip install --only-deps .` installs from it,
  and it ignores `uv.lock`.

With an exact pin in `pyproject.toml`,
the declared version and the locked version are the same,
and a version only changes when someone changes the pin.
That change shows up in the diff of `pyproject.toml`,
where reviewers will see it.

A **package**, the kind of project you will build in the
[packaging chapters](1110-packaging.qmd),
is the opposite case.
A package gets installed into *other people's* environments,
next to whatever versions of pandas their projects already use.
Exact pins there would make your package impossible to install alongside theirs,
so packages declare ranges and leave the exact choice to the project that installs them.

| Kind of project | Declares | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data analysis (an application) | exact versions, `pandas==3.1.1` | The result depends on the exact versions, and nobody installs it into another environment |
| Package (a library) | ranges, `pandas>=3.0` | It has to fit into other people's environments |

## Making `uv add` write exact versions

`uv` has a setting for this.
Add a `[tool.uv]` table to `pyproject.toml`:

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
```

That table and comment are taken from the
[docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv) example project
(MIT license), which the container chapters build on.

From then on, `uv add` writes `==`.
Here is the same project after removing pandas and adding it again:

```bash
uv remove pandas
uv add pandas
```

```out
Resolved 1 package in 5ms
Uninstalled 4 packages in 200ms
 - numpy==2.5.5
 - pandas==3.1.1
 - python-dateutil==4.0.0
 - tzdata==2026.6
Resolved 5 packages in 7ms
Installed 4 packages in 29ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
```

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
name = "pins-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pandas==3.1.1",
]

[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
```

The setting lives in `pyproject.toml`,
so everyone on the project gets the same behavior from `uv add`.

For a single command,
`uv add --bounds exact pandas` does the same thing without the setting.
`--bounds` also accepts `lower` (the default), `major` and `minor`,
which write wider ranges.

:::{.callout-warning title="Existing lower bounds do not change"}
The setting only changes what `uv add` writes *from now on*.
Running `uv add pandas` again in a project that already has `pandas>=3.1.1`
leaves that line as it is.

To convert a package you already have,
look up the version you are using
and add it again with that version:

```bash
uv tree --depth 1
```

```out
Resolved 6 packages in 13ms
penguin-analysis v0.1.0
├── palmerpenguins v0.1.6
└── pandas v3.1.1
```

```bash
uv add "pandas==3.1.1" "palmerpenguins==0.1.6"
```
:::

## Changing a pinned version

With an exact pin,
`uv lock --upgrade-package pandas` cannot move pandas,
because `pyproject.toml` only allows one version.
To move it, change the pin:

```bash
uv add "pandas==3.0.5"
```

```out
Resolved 5 packages in 118ms
Downloading pandas (9.5MiB)
 Downloaded pandas
Prepared 1 package in 1.16s
Uninstalled 1 package in 100ms
Installed 1 package in 14ms
 - pandas==3.1.1
 + pandas==3.0.5
```

One command updates `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and `.venv/` together,
and the commit that changes the pin is the record of when and why it moved.

The packages you did not name,
such as `numpy` and `python-dateutil` here,
are still pinned exactly, but only in `uv.lock`.
`uv lock --upgrade-package numpy` moves one of them,
as in [uv: sharing and managing an environment](0535-virtual-environments-python-uv-sharing.qmd).

## The same idea in R

R projects declare their packages in a `DESCRIPTION` file,
and this book pins those exactly too:

```{.default filename="DESCRIPTION"}
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1)
```

`DESCRIPTION` with `==` plays the part of `pyproject.toml` with `add-bounds = "exact"`,
and `renv.lock` plays the part of `uv.lock`.
[renv: declaring packages in `DESCRIPTION`](0565-virtual-environments-r-renv-description.qmd)
shows how.
